I find it difficult to understand why attendance is enforced in a course conducted in this manner, and even more difficult to justify its direct impact on grading. Penalizing students for not attending—or for being unable to attend—is fundamentally unfair. Academic evaluation should be based on learning outcomes, effort, and demonstrated understanding, not on physical presence.

Students learn in different ways: some benefit from attending lectures, some learn more effectively through independent study, and others may attend without engaging meaningfully with the material. Using attendance as a graded requirement—especially as an implicit threat to students’ grades—is an ineffective and unnecessary approach to promoting learning. Forcing attendance through grade penalties does not encourage genuine engagement; it merely inflates physical presence without improving academic quality.

Moreover, mandatory attendance actively disrupts the learning environment. Students who attend solely to sign the attendance sheet often arrive late, interrupt the lecture, and engage in activities unrelated to the course. These interruptions distract students who are genuinely trying to follow the lesson. Being interrupted by requests for signatures or movement in the classroom significantly reduces concentration and breaks the continuity of the lecture.

Eliminating mandatory attendance would not reduce academic standards. On the contrary, it would enhance the overall quality of the course by allowing motivated students to engage without constant disruption, while respecting individual learning preferences and circumstances. Attendance-based enforcement, particularly when tied to grades, is unnecessary and counterproductive in a higher-education setting and should be reconsidered to improve both fairness and instructional effectiveness.
